title: [SSH]  add TShark ssh.textonly field for "exec" and "shell" request
description:
**EDIT following to !20248 !20249 !20273 and !20283 - 2026-03-22**  
## This MR add a new field to TShark which print ASCII / UTF-8 part of decrypted payload for "exec" and "shell"  request
This MR to solve issue: https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/issues/20580 (which is more a **feature request** than an issue... )   

The idea of this MR is to let TShark print the 'data-text-lines' dissector when it's used to display UTF-8 decrypted text in Wireshark, as today TShark only display hexencoded decrypted payload which is perfect to print binaries but not user friendly when printing UTF-8 text   


### New added field: 
```bash
 -e ssh.textonly 
```
  
This MR can be used to easily follow command and command results in an interactive ssh terminal session:  
- on the left `ssh` command 
- on the right `tshark` decryption command using `-T fields -e ssh.textonly -E aggregator=$'\n' -E escape=n`  
  (aggregator is used to avoid `sed` or other terminal postprocessing) 
  
![image](/uploads/96ef496bf1ce4ffc0a302f0b00fad799/image.png){width=900 height=271}
  
The idea is to make UTF-8 becomes human readable in the same way it's displayed in Wireshark UI:  
  
![Capture_d_écran_du_2026-03-22_11-17-27](/uploads/18b19dec34c2be81770aae36d2929653/Capture_d_écran_du_2026-03-22_11-17-27.png){width=900 height=475}

**END EDIT**   

---------------------------
---------------------------   


Original MR description:
## ASCII FIELD ADDITION

**All captures and traces of the issue had been provides directly in the issues.**  

**Here will only be posted a final capture where ascii part of decrypted payload is directly printed and readable by the user.**     

### Captures:  

#### Capture command

```bash
/usr/src/build/wireshark/build/run/tshark \
        -i enp0s3 \
        -n \
        -o ssh.keylog_file:/home/nba/ascii_field.keylog \
        -o ssh.debug_file:/home/nba/ascii_field.debug \
        -o ssh.desegment_buffers:TRUE \
        -o tcp.desegment_tcp_streams:TRUE \
        -o tcp.reassemble_out_of_order:TRUE \
        -t ad \
        -l \
        -f '(host 10.0.50.78 or host 10.0.50.91) and (host 10.0.50.77 or host 10.0.50.75) and port 22' \
        -T fields \
        -e frame.number \
        -e frame.time_relative \
        -e ip.src \
        -e ip.dst \
        -e tcp.srcport \
        -e tcp.dstport \
        -e tcp.len \
        -e _ws.col.Protocol \
        -e _ws.col.Info  \
        -e ssh.cookie \
        -e ssh.message_code \
        -e ssh.ascii_decrypted_payload \
        --log-level noisy \
        --log-domain packet-ssh 
        -w ascii_field.pcap


```

#### Test command

```bash
/usr/src/build/openssh-portable/ssh -F none -o KexAlgorithms=mlkem768x25519-sha256 -o Ciphers=chacha20-poly1305@openssh.com  nba@10.0.50.77 ls / 2>&1 >/dev/null
```

The loop as written is unacceptable. It does not verify that the input is valid UTF-8. You *must* ensure that it is before calling `proto_tree_add_string()` (see https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/blob/master/doc/README.developer#L649-655)

Even though this will have passed decryption and MAC checks, presumably (which reduces some of the fuzzing concerns) since the character set for client data is not specified in the SSH protocol anywhere, it is *probably* UTF-8 in the original but not necessarily.

You can do something like `tvb_get_string_enc(pinfo->pool, next_tvb, off, len, ENC_UTF_8);` add those to a string array (`char**`) and then call `wmem_strjoinv(pinfo->pool, '\n', str_array)`. (The latter is from wsutil/str_util.h).

Of the approaches above, the GLib approach is cleaner. wmem also provides a resizable array (wmem_array), which can be used with pointers (though it's more similar to GArray and lacks some of the nice for dealing with pointers functions that GPtrArray adds, it does have a function to set to always automatically have a null terminator), but GPtrArray is good. (For the C99 approach, I would prefer using `wmem_realloc` to re-implementing it.)

Recent versions of GLib add support for automatically terminating a GPtrArray (>= 2.74), and add GStrvBuilder (>= 2.68) which might be even more relevant for your approach, but those are past the Wireshark minimum requirements now so let's not use those I guess.

Another similar approach would be to repeatedly append to a GString or wmem_strbuf, though the more Python build an array and then join it approach is fine.

I guess the point of what you're doing (rather than just getting one big string) is universal line termination, replacing '\r\n' with '\n' if that is present. It might be helpful to have a comment to that effect.
